A.explanation: This is lower than both starting densities and ignores that mass is conserved when $1.5 \text{ m}^3$ of water and $0.50 \text{ m}^3$ of alcohol are added.

B.explanation: This is the simple volume-weighted mean of $1000$ and $800$, which wrongly weights by volume instead of finding total mass divided by $2.0 \text{ m}^3$.

C.explanation: This value is close but does not equal the total mass of $1900 \text{ kg}$ divided by the mixture volume of $2.0 \text{ m}^3$.

D.explanation: Total mass $1500 \text{ kg} + 400 \text{ kg} = 1900 \text{ kg}$ divided by $2.0 \text{ m}^3$ gives $950 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

hints: Notice you are given two separate volumes, $1.5 \text{ m}^3$ and $0.50 \text{ m}^3$, with different densities, so you cannot just average $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and $800 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
Recall $\rho = m/V$, so rearrange to $m = \rho V$ to find the mass of water and the mass of alcohol separately before mixing.
Add the two masses to get total mass, then divide by the given mixture volume of $2.0 \text{ m}^3$ to get mixture density.
walkthrough: Identify the conserved quantity: mass adds, so find $m = \rho V$ for each liquid. Water mass is $m_w = 1000 \times 1.5 = 1500 \text{ kg}$.
Add to get total mass in the mixture: $m = 1500 + 400 = 1900 \text{ kg}$.
Use the mixture volume $V = 2.0 \text{ m}^3$ in $\rho = m/V$: $\rho = 1900 / 2.0 = 950 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
